title: NASA's X-59 Pulls Off Dizzying Stunts — and It's Designed to Replace Sonic Booms With a Gentle 'Thump'
summary: Imagine a jet that slices through the sky faster than sound, yet instead of a deafening sonic boom, it produces only a soft 'thump' — no louder than a car door closing. That's the promise of NASA's X-59 Quiet SuperSonic Technology (QueSST) aircraft, and a newly released video shows it performing its most daring acrobatics to date. During a test flight on April 14 over California's Mojave Desert, the needle-nosed plane executed dizzying ascensions and precise axial turns — maneuvers that look intense even on screen. It reached Mach 0.95, roughly 730 miles per hour, just shy of breaking the sound barrier. But the real milestone is what comes next: supersonic flight without the traditional sonic boom. The X-59 is a collaboration between NASA and Lockheed Martin, over a decade in the making. It was unveiled in January 2025 and first flew that October. Since then, it has completed nine more flights, each pushing closer to its design goals. When it finally hits its cruising speed of Mach 1.42 (about 940 mph) at 55,000 feet, the aircraft is engineered to produce a 'sonic thump' with a perceived loudness of around 75 PLdB. That's roughly 16 times quieter than the Concorde's notorious booms, which led to bans on overland supersonic flight. 'Moving forward, the X-59 will continue to test its performance at high and fast test points as well as low and slow test points,' Lockheed said in a recent update. The joint team then plans to 'move quickly into supersonic speeds and eventually the aircraft's design points of roughly 55,000 feet and Mach 1.4, where it will create the first ever quiet supersonic thump.' If successful, this technology could rewrite aviation rules, allowing commercial supersonic jets to fly over populated areas without disturbing people below. While NASA and Lockheed have hyped the X-59 as a path to faster commercial air travel, the military is also eyeing the next-generation plane for its own purposes. For now, though, the X-59's acrobatic test flights are a thrilling preview of a future where crossing continents in half the time might come with just a gentle thump outside your window.
why_it_matters: If the X-59 succeeds, it could usher in a new era of quiet supersonic airliners that slash long‑distance travel times in half, potentially making the world feel smaller — but only if noise and environmental concerns are solved.

background_read: In 1973, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration banned civilian supersonic flight over land because sonic booms shattered windows and frightened people.
The Concorde (the iconic supersonic passenger jet that flew from 1976 to 2003) could only fly at top speed over the ocean, severely limiting its routes.
NASA’s X-59 is the first aircraft built from the ground up to reshape shockwaves into a soft thump, potentially lifting the decades-old ban.
Testing happens over California’s Mojave Desert (an arid, sparsely populated region long used for secret aircraft trials), providing a safe space for these high‑risk maneuvers.
If the X-59 proves its quiet thump works, international regulators could rewrite noise rules, opening the door for fast, overland passenger jets.

perspectives.description: A successful quiet thump could let airlines cut a New York‑to‑London flight to under three hours, boosting tourism and business. Manufacturers see a huge market for fast, overland supersonic jets.

Even a soft thump may disturb sleep or startle wildlife. Supersonic jets burn far more fuel per passenger, increasing greenhouse gas emissions, so some groups argue the environmental cost outweighs the time savings.

Noise regulations have shaped aviation since the 1970s. The Concorde’s ocean‑only routes show how public tolerance and policy can make or break a technology. The X-59 is a deliberate attempt to rewrite those rules.

If the quiet thump proves acceptable, regulators could define new noise standards within a decade, sparking a race among aircraft manufacturers to build the next generation of eco‑friendlier, high‑speed airliners.
